scenarios.title: Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.domains: D1 Agentic Architecture · D2 Tool Design & MCP · D5 Context & Reliability
scenarios.brief: A home-goods retailer runs its support agent on the Claude Agent SDK, handling about 18,000 tickets a week. The agent calls custom MCP tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human and issue_store_credit. It may refund up to $500 per order; larger refunds need a human's approval. Returns are accepted within 30 days. First-contact resolution is 68% against an 80% target.

scenarios.title: Scenario 2 — Code Generation with Claude Code
scenarios.domains: D3 Claude Code Configuration & Workflows · D5 Context & Reliability · D4 Prompt Engineering
scenarios.brief: A 40-engineer platform team uses Claude Code in a monorepo with services/ (Go), web/ (React + TypeScript) and infra/ (Terraform). Team configuration is committed under .claude/, including path-scoped rules and skills, and several engineers keep personal ~/.claude/ setups. Eight contractors have just joined. The current large task is an API migration codemod touching about 70 files across two trees.

questions.question: The agent's control loop stops when the latest reply contains a closing line such as "Is there anything else I can help with?" or when fifteen iterations have passed. The incident log shows two patterns. Some tickets end with a refund half-done: in each, the final response opened with a courteous wrap-up sentence and then carried a request to run process_refund. Other tickets, mostly multi-order returns, reach fifteen and are cut off. Their transcripts show each step calling a different tool and building on the result before it. What is the root cause?

options.t: The fifteen-step ceiling is too low for multi-order returns and should be raised, with a limit per ticket type set from observed step counts.
options.why: Incorrect. A higher cap would let the long tickets finish, but the cap would still be the main way the loop stops, and the half-done refunds would continue. Iteration caps are a runaway guard, not the stop signal.

options.t: The loop judges that a turn is finished from the reply's wording and a counter, instead of from the stop reason returned with each response.
options.why: Correct. A response that requests a tool comes back with stop_reason "tool_use" whatever its text says; the loop should continue on that and stop on "end_turn". Both failure patterns come from ignoring that field.

options.t: Tool results are not being added back into the message history, so the model loses track of finished steps and keeps requesting them.
options.why: Runner-up. Missing tool results in history do make an agent repeat itself until it hits a cap. It would win if the capped transcripts showed the same lookup repeated; here each step calls a different tool and builds on the last result.

options.t: The wrap-up detector needs a broader phrase list and should skip any response that also contains a request to run a tool.
options.why: Incorrect. Skipping responses with tool requests patches one symptom, but completion is still inferred from text, which the exam guide lists as an anti-pattern, and the cap problem remains.

questions.decider: The capped transcripts show each step calling a different tool and building on the previous result; if they showed the same lookup repeated, missing tool results in history would be the cause.
questions.explanation: The agentic loop continues while stop_reason is "tool_use" and ends on "end_turn". Parsing the reply's text for a closing phrase and using an iteration cap as the primary stop are both listed anti-patterns; a cap belongs only as a safety guard.

eli5.question: The agent's loop decides when a ticket is finished, and it gets that wrong in two ways. The clue is: the half-done refunds all ended on a reply that still asked to run a tool, and the long tickets were making real progress at every step. So the question is about how the loop knows a turn is over, not about the size of the limit.
eli5.answer: Think of a waiter who leaves the table as soon as someone says "thanks", even while they are still ordering. The API already tells you, with every reply, whether Claude wants a tool run or is done (the stop_reason: tool_use or end_turn). The loop should read that label, not the polite words and not a step counter. A step limit can stay, but only as a safety stop for runaways. Rule: keep going on tool_use, stop on end_turn; never judge "done" from the text.
options: A bigger step limit lets long tickets finish, but the limit is still deciding when to stop, and the half-done refunds keep happening.
Correct. Read the stop reason on each reply instead of guessing from words or counting steps.

Runner-up. If tool results were missing from the history (the agent's record of what came back), it would repeat itself until the limit. It would win if the long transcripts showed the same lookup again and again.
A longer list of goodbye phrases still guesses "done" from text, and it does nothing for the long tickets.

deep.premise: It is tempting to treat this as two bugs with two fixes: a phrase detector that misfires and a limit that is too low. Both come from one design mistake. The loop is guessing whether Claude has finished, from wording and from a counter, when every API response already says so in its stop_reason field. A reply can say goodbye and still ask for a tool in the same turn.

questions.question: issue_store_credit went live six weeks ago. Since then, 31% of customers who asked for their money back on a damaged item have received a voucher instead, and finance has flagged the voucher spend. Most of these chats open with a long account of a bad experience, such as a ruined birthday gift or a wasted afternoon. The new tool's description reads "Compensate a customer for a poor experience." and process_refund's reads "Refund a customer's order." Which change is the most effective first step?

options.t: Add four or five sample conversations to the system prompt in which an upset customer asks for their money and the agent calls process_refund.
options.why: Runner-up. Examples can steer selection, and they would be the next lever if the two descriptions already drew a clear boundary. Here the descriptions are one-liners that both fit an upset customer, so examples treat the symptom and add tokens.

options.t: Merge the two into a single remedy tool with a remedy-type parameter, chosen after the agent confirms what the customer asked for.
options.why: Incorrect. Consolidation is a redesign that changes the agent's tool contract; it is more effort than a first step and moves the same ambiguity into a parameter.

options.t: Rewrite both descriptions to state what each remedy is for, the input it takes, and which requests belong to the other tool.
options.why: Correct. Descriptions are the main signal for tool choice. "Poor experience" matches almost every damaged-item chat, and neither description says when not to use it. Stating purpose and boundaries is the cheap, high-leverage first fix.

options.t: Add a routing step that classifies each request as refund or credit from its wording and exposes only the matching tool.
options.why: Incorrect. A wording-based router is extra machinery and is itself a keyword heuristic; it is over-engineered before the descriptions have been fixed.

questions.decider: The two descriptions are single sentences and 'poor experience' covers nearly every damaged-item chat; if the descriptions already stated clear boundaries, adding examples of upset customers would be the next step.
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism for tool selection, and they are read against each other. When two tools overlap in purpose, each description must say what it is for and which requests belong to the other tool before reaching for examples, routers or consolidation.

eli5.question: Customers who want their money back are getting vouchers. The clue is: the two tool descriptions are one short sentence each, and "poor experience" fits almost every damaged-item chat. The upset stories are the distraction.
eli5.answer: Picture two drawers labelled only "Make it up to them" and "Give money back". A helper facing an upset customer will often open the first one. Labels that say what each drawer is for, and when to use the other one, fix that at the source (tool descriptions). They are the main thing Claude reads when choosing a tool, and rewriting them is cheap. Rule: when two tools get mixed up, fix their descriptions first.
options: Runner-up. Showing worked chats (few-shot examples) can steer the choice. It would be the next step if the labels were already clear; here they are not.
Merging the tools into one is a redesign. It is too big for a first step and moves the confusion into a setting.
Correct. Clear descriptions with boundaries fix the overlap where it starts.
A word-matching router is extra machinery and is itself a keyword guess.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the emotional stories are the cause, so the agent needs examples of upset customers who still want a refund. The stories only expose the real weakness: the two descriptions overlap. "Compensate a customer for a poor experience" describes nearly every damaged-item chat, and neither description says when not to use it. Descriptions are the main signal Claude uses to choose a tool, so they come first.

questions.question: The $500 ceiling lives in one sentence of the system prompt. Last quarter seven refunds between $520 and $1,340 went out without approval; in each transcript the agent mentioned the ceiling, then judged the case exceptional, such as a damaged wedding gift or a customer threatening to cancel a membership. Finance now classes any unapproved refund above the ceiling as a reportable control failure, and those cases must still reach a person with context rather than stall. Which change best fits the requirement?

options.t: Rewrite the escalation section with explicit criteria for over-limit cases and add two or three examples of declining and escalating.
options.why: Runner-up. Explicit criteria plus examples is the recommended way to calibrate escalation judgement. It would win if the goal were to reduce exceptions; finance's control-failure rule needs a deterministic block, and prompts have a non-zero failure rate.

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook on process_refund that checks each issued amount and opens an escalation when it is above $500.
options.why: Incorrect. A PostToolUse hook sees the result after the refund has gone out, so it reports the violation instead of preventing it.

options.t: Set tool_choice to force escalate_to_human on any turn where the order total from lookup_order is above $500.
options.why: Incorrect. The order total is not the refund amount, so this escalates small refunds on large orders and misses nothing it should catch more reliably; tool_choice controls which tool is called, not what amount is allowed.

options.t: Add a PreToolUse hook on process_refund that denies amounts above $500 and tells the agent to escalate.
options.why: Correct. A hook inspects every outgoing refund call and blocks the policy violation in code, then redirects the agent to escalate_to_human, so the customer still reaches a person.

questions.decider: Finance treats any unapproved refund above $500 as a reportable control failure, which needs a deterministic block; if the aim were only to reduce exceptions, explicit criteria with examples would be the proportionate fix.
questions.explanation: When compliance must be deterministic, prompt instructions are not enough because they have a non-zero failure rate. A hook that intercepts the outgoing tool call can block the violation and redirect the agent to escalation.

eli5.question: Refunds above the $500 limit keep going out. The clue is: finance now treats every single one as a reportable failure. That means the limit must hold every time, not most of the time.
eli5.answer: A sign on the till saying "no refunds over $500" works most days, but staff with a sad story in front of them sometimes break it. A till that refuses the amount works every day. In the agent, that till is a check that runs before every refund call (a PreToolUse hook). It blocks the call and tells the agent to escalate, so the customer still reaches a person. Rule: if it must hold every time, enforce it in code, not in the prompt.
options: Runner-up. Clearer rules plus examples is the right way to improve judgement. It would win if the goal were fewer exceptions, not zero.
A check that runs after the call (PostToolUse hook) sees the refund once the money has already gone.
Forcing a tool (tool_choice) picks which tool runs, not what amount is allowed, and an order total is not a refund amount.
Correct. A check before every refund call blocks over-limit amounts and sends the case to a person.

deep.premise: It is tempting to read the transcripts and think the agent needs better judgement: it saw the limit and talked itself past it. Better criteria and examples would reduce that. But finance's rule changes the question from "reduce" to "must not happen". A prompt, however good, has a non-zero failure rate. Only code that runs on every refund call can hold a hard limit, and it can still hand the case to a person.

questions.question: Escalation fires when a sentiment score over the customer's messages crosses a frustration threshold. A labelled review of 400 tickets found two kinds of error. Customers who typed in capitals about a late parcel, which a tracking lookup would have settled, were passed to a person at once; one supervisor calls these 'the shouting queue'. Customers who wrote politely that they would like to speak to someone stayed with the agent for several more turns. Which change most improves escalation decisions?

options.t: Escalate on stated triggers, namely the customer asks for a person, policy does not cover the case, or the agent cannot progress, and drop the score.
options.why: Correct. Escalation should rest on categorical triggers, with an explicit request for a person honoured at once. Sentiment is an unreliable proxy for whether a case needs a human.

options.t: Resolve straightforward issues whatever the customer's tone, and hand over only if the customer repeats a request for a person after a fix is offered.
options.why: Runner-up. Offering a resolution first is right for a frustrated customer with a simple problem, which fixes the shouting queue. It fails the polite customers: an explicit request for a person should be honoured immediately, not after a second ask.

options.t: Re-fit the frustration threshold on the 400 labelled tickets and refresh it monthly as more reviewed tickets come in.
options.why: Incorrect. A better-tuned threshold is still a sentiment threshold; calm requests for a person and angry simple questions sit on the wrong sides of any cut-off.

options.t: Train a classifier on past tickets labelled escalate or resolve and use its prediction in place of the sentiment score.
options.why: Incorrect. A trained classifier is heavy machinery for a problem that clear criteria solve, and it inherits whatever inconsistency is in the historic labels.

questions.decider: Polite customers who said they would like to speak to someone were kept with the agent; if the only error were angry customers with simple problems, offering a fix first and escalating on a repeat request would be enough.
questions.explanation: Escalation triggers are categorical: an explicit request for a human (honoured immediately), a policy exception or gap, or inability to progress. Sentiment and self-reported confidence are unreliable proxies for case complexity.

eli5.question: Escalation is driven by how angry the customer sounds, and it is wrong both ways. The clue is: polite customers who asked to speak to someone were kept waiting. The "shouting queue" is the vivid part, but fixing only that leaves the polite requests unanswered.
eli5.answer: A shop that calls the manager only when a customer raises their voice gets two things wrong. Loud customers with easy problems get the manager, and quiet customers who ask for the manager do not. Instead, use clear reasons to hand over (escalation triggers): the customer asks for a person, the policy does not cover the case, or the agent is stuck. An explicit request is honoured at once. Rule: escalate on what the case needs, not on how the customer sounds.
options: Correct. Clear triggers, with a request for a person honoured straight away.
Runner-up. Offering a fix first is right for an angry customer with an easy problem. It would win if no one had asked for a person; asking should be honoured at once.
A better-tuned anger score (sentiment threshold) still measures tone, not need.
A trained classifier is heavy machinery for a problem that clear rules solve.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the shouting queue is the main problem, so the fix is to ignore tone and offer a resolution first. That fixes half of it. The polite customers show the other half: they asked for a person, and an explicit request should be honoured immediately, not after a second ask. Both errors come from using sentiment, which is an unreliable stand-in for what a case needs.

questions.question: get_customer is called with the name the customer gives. For common names it often finds several records; it then returns the one with the most recent order, with a match_confidence that averages 0.61 in those cases. About one such lookup in four lands on the wrong account, which is noticed only when a refund reaches a stranger's card. Roughly 80% of chats start in the guest widget on the order-tracking page, before any sign-in. What should happen when a lookup returns several records?

options.t: Use the account linked to the email or phone number the chat session came from, and fall back to the name lookup only when none exists.
options.why: Runner-up. A verified contact on the session is better than any name match, and it would win if chats arrived tied to an account. Most chats here start as guests, so the fallback still guesses on most of them.

options.t: Pass on the top match only when its score clears 0.85, and send lower-scoring lookups to escalate_to_human with the candidate list.
options.why: Incorrect. A higher threshold still selects heuristically above it, and routing the rest to humans hurts first-contact resolution when one question to the customer would settle it.

options.t: Return every matching record and have the agent ask the customer for an order number or postcode before acting.
options.why: Correct. With several matches, the deciding fact is something only the customer knows. Asking for an identifier replaces a guess with a lookup and costs one turn.

options.t: Rank candidates by recent orders and city, then have the agent read the chosen name and city back to the customer to confirm.
options.why: Incorrect. This is still heuristic selection; a customer with the same common name in the same city will confirm the wrong record.

questions.decider: About 80% of chats start in the guest widget before any sign-in, so most have no linked account; if chats arrived tied to a verified account, using that account would beat asking.
questions.explanation: When several customer records match, ask the customer for an identifier rather than choosing heuristically. A confidence score attached to a guess does not make it a reliable identification.

eli5.question: A name search finds several customers, and the system picks one by guessing. The clue is: most chats start as guests, before anyone signs in, so there is usually no account linked to the chat. The confidence number is a distraction.
eli5.answer: If a parcel arrives for "J. Smith" in a building with three J. Smiths, you do not hand it to the one who ordered most recently. You ask for the flat number. Here, the agent should say it found several matches and ask the customer for something that tells them apart, such as an order number or postcode (ask for identifiers). One question replaces a one-in-four guess. Rule: several matches means ask the customer, not pick for them.
options: Runner-up. Using the account the chat is signed in to (session identity) beats any name match. It would win if chats came with a signed-in account; most here are guests.
A stricter cut-off (confidence threshold) still guesses above it and sends the rest to people unnecessarily.
Correct. Return all matches and ask for an order number or postcode.
Reading the guess back is still a guess; another J. Smith in the same city will say yes.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the lookup needs a better way to choose: a higher threshold, a better ranking, or another signal such as the chat's account. But when several records match a name, the deciding fact is not in the system at all. It is in the customer's head. The reliable move is to ask for an identifier. A verified account on the chat would also settle it, but most of these chats do not have one.

questions.question: About 14% of tickets are follow-ups on a case the agent already handled. The agent gets the earlier contact as a prose paragraph from a summarisation pass, inserted after the 5,000-token returns policy and before the new message; a typical one reads "Customer was offered a partial refund and seemed satisfied." On follow-ups the agent quotes refund figures that differ from what was paid and repeats offers already made. A promised Friday callback and a replacement held for restock appear in no system of record, only in the earlier chat. Which TWO changes together make follow-ups reliable?

options.t: Replace the prose with a structured case record holding customer ID, order ID, amount paid, dates, offers made and open commitments.
options.why: Correct. Summarisation turned exact amounts and commitments into "partial refund" and "seemed satisfied". A record of transactional facts carries the values the agent must act on.

options.t: Have the agent call lookup_order at the start of each follow-up and rebuild the case history from the order's records.
options.why: Runner-up. Re-reading the system of record is good when the facts live there. The callback and the held replacement exist only in the earlier chat, so the order record cannot rebuild them.

options.t: Raise the summariser's output limit and let each summary describe the earlier contact in more detail.
options.why: Incorrect. Longer prose is still prose: it still paraphrases amounts and commitments, and it still lands in the middle of a long context.

options.t: Load the case record first in the context under its own heading, ahead of the policy text and the new message.
options.why: Correct. The summary currently sits between a 5,000-token policy block and the new message, where models read least reliably. Key facts belong at the start with a clear heading.

options.t: Resume the earlier conversation's session when the customer returns and continue with its full transcript and tool results.
options.why: Incorrect. Resuming brings back stale tool results from a week ago; a fresh start seeded with a structured summary is more reliable.

questions.decider: The callback and the held replacement exist only in the earlier chat, and the summary sits in the middle of a long context; if every commitment lived in the order system, re-reading the order would replace the structured record.
questions.explanation: Progressive summarisation turns exact numbers and commitments into vague prose. Extract transactional facts into a persistent case-facts block and place it at the start of the context under an explicit heading, where it is read reliably.

eli5.question: On follow-up tickets the agent gets the facts wrong. The clue is in two places: the summary is vague prose, and it sits in the middle of a long block of policy text. Also, some promises exist only in the earlier chat, so no system can rebuild them.
eli5.answer: Picture a nurse handing over a patient with "seemed fine, had some medicine" scribbled in the middle of a thick binder. The next nurse needs exact doses and times, on the front page. So keep the facts as a filled-in form, not a story (structured case-facts block), and put it first under a clear heading, where it gets read (start of the context). Rule: exact facts in a structured block, placed first.
options: Correct. A record with exact IDs, amounts, dates and promises keeps what prose summaries blur.
Runner-up. Re-reading the order system is good when the facts live there. The callback and the held replacement exist only in the old chat.
A longer summary is still a story; it still blurs numbers and still sits in the middle.
Correct. Put the record first, under its own heading, not buried after 5,000 tokens of policy.
Resuming the old session brings back week-old tool results; a fresh start with a structured summary is more reliable.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the agent just needs more of the history: a longer summary, the old session, or a fresh lookup. The problem is not quantity. Summarisation turned exact facts (amount paid, promised callback) into "partial refund" and "seemed satisfied", and what survived sits in the middle of a long context, the spot models read least reliably. Two things must change together: the form of the facts and their position.

questions.question: To make behaviour predictable, an architect proposes replacing the agentic loop with a fixed decision tree: classify each ticket into one of fourteen categories, then run a hard-coded tool sequence for that category. On last month's tickets the tree slightly beats the agent on the top six categories, which are 62% of volume and each follow one known path. It does noticeably worse on the other eight, where most tickets raise more than one concern or need a step that depends on what the order lookup shows. What does this pilot best support?

options.t: Run fixed sequences for the six single-path categories and send every other ticket, multi-concern ones included, to the loop.
options.why: Correct. Fixed sequences suit work whose path is known in advance; the model-driven loop suits work whose next step depends on what was just found. The pilot shows both kinds in one workload.

options.t: Keep the loop for every ticket and have it split multi-concern messages into separate concerns, investigated in parallel.
options.why: Runner-up. Decomposing multi-concern requests is recommended and helps the long tail. It would win if the tree showed no gain anywhere; here it is better on 62% of volume that follows one known path.

options.t: Grow the tree to about forty categories, give long-tail tickets their own hard-coded sequences, and rerun the pilot on last month's tickets.
options.why: Incorrect. More categories cannot hard-code a step that depends on what a lookup returns, and multi-concern tickets do not fit a single category.

options.t: Move the classifier after the order lookup and let it choose the sequence using the order data as well as the ticket text.
options.why: Incorrect. Better classification inputs do not help tickets whose path branches part-way through or that carry several concerns.

questions.decider: The tree beats the agent on the top six categories, 62% of volume with one known path each; if it showed no gain on any category, keeping the loop everywhere and decomposing multi-concern tickets would be the better design.
questions.explanation: Model-driven loops and pre-configured sequences suit different work. A fixed sequence wins where the path is knowable in advance; the loop wins where the next step depends on what was just found, including multi-concern requests that need decomposition.

For a dinner where you decide what to cook after opening the fridge, you need a cook who thinks (model-driven agentic loop). This workload has both kinds. Use the fixed sequence where the path is known and the loop where the next step depends on what is found. Rule: fixed steps for known paths, the agent loop for paths that depend on results.

options.why: Runner-up. A directory CLAUDE.md is a fine home when a convention belongs to one directory tree. These tests and helpers span two trees, so this needs two copies to keep in step, where one glob covers both.

options.why: Runner-up. An independent reviewer beats self-review, and it would win if the review ran inside the session that wrote the code. The CI job already starts fresh on a clean checkout, so it is independent.

options.t: Run the review with --output-format json and a findings schema, and post each finding as an inline PR comment.
options.why: Incorrect. Machine-readable findings improve how the review is delivered, not what a single pass notices; the thin middle and the missed caller remain.

options.t: Add the team's review criteria and the new API's contract to CLAUDE.md, giving the CI reviewer more project context to work from.
options.why: Incorrect. CLAUDE.md is the right home for review criteria, but more context does not help a single pass that is already spread thin across 70 files.

options.t: Review each changed file alone for local correctness, then run one pass over the interfaces and call sites between files.
options.why: Correct. Per-file passes give each file full attention, and a separate integration pass looks specifically at contracts between files, which is where the missed caller lives.

questions.decider: The review already runs as claude -p on a clean checkout, so it is independent of the generating session; if it ran in the session that wrote the codemod, a separate instance would be the first fix.
questions.explanation: Large multi-file changes need two kinds of review: per-file passes for local correctness and a cross-file integration pass for contracts between files. One pass over everything dilutes attention.

eli5.question: One review over 70 files goes thin in the middle and misses a mismatch between two files. The clue is: the review already runs in CI as a separate, fresh process. So it is already independent; the problem is doing everything in one pass.
eli5.answer: One inspector checking a 70-room building in one walk gets tired by the middle and never checks whether the pipes between rooms connect. Better: check each room on its own, then do one walk just for the connections. For code, that is a pass per file plus a cross-file pass (multi-pass review). Rule: big changes get per-file passes plus one integration pass.

deep.premise: It is tempting to read the lead's remark and think the reviewer is biased because it is too close to the code. But claude -p on a clean checkout is already a separate instance with none of the generating session's reasoning. The symptoms point elsewhere: thin in the middle means attention spread over 70 files, and a missed caller means nobody looked at the connections between files.
